paras: The threatened lynching of Jesse Myers and Frank Brown took place at New Madrid, Missouri, in late May 1881, when a mob organized to hang the two men, accused members of an outlaw gang, after they were brought to the town jail. Before the mob could act, Sheriff Walters and a few assistants removed the prisoners after dark and took them by river to St. Louis. The threat arose during a widely reported manhunt in southeast Missouri; Myers and Brown were later tried and hanged legally at New Madrid on July 15, 1881.

According to the Sedalia Weekly Bazoo, Myers, Brown, James Hamilton and Pat Rhodes lived together near Bain's store, nine miles from New Madrid, and were suspected of local thefts. On May 8 a volley fired into farmer William Knox's house wounded a visitor named Coleman and killed an infant he was carrying. When Sheriff Walters's posse tried to arrest the four, posse member La Ferge (Laforge in Memphis) was shot dead.

In Wayne County, Sheriff John T. Davis and ex-Sheriff James F. Hatton were shot while trying to arrest Myers and Hamilton near Greenville. Hundreds of armed citizens joined the hunt; a party under Col. W. T. Leeper ambushed the pair at Campbell's Switch, killing Hamilton and wounding Myers, and Brown was taken the same day. Rhodes, found wounded earlier, was sent back under guard but "never reached Sikeston," according to a Minnesota paper; the coverage does not show what became of him.

Myers and Brown were brought to the New Madrid jail on a Sunday evening, according to a Madrid Bend, Kentucky, correspondent of the Hickman Courier writing on May 24. Shortly after dark, he wrote, "Judge Lynch was organizing his court to hang them in haste and try them at leisure." The sheriff and two or three assistants took the prisoners around the town to the river, rowed them three miles downstream in a skiff, and put them aboard the steamer Colorado for St. Louis.

A wire paragraph said Sheriff Walters "eluded lynching parties at New Madrid" and took his prisoners to Cairo by steamer, and that officers reached St. Louis with Myers, Brown and Mitchell. The Sedalia account said Mitchell, a young acquaintance, had been jailed as an accomplice, and that public excitement ran so high that the sheriff removed the prisoners one night. The New Madrid Record and a Poplar Bluff dispatch instead attributed the removal to Governor Crittenden's order to hold the men in St. Louis until trial.

A special grand jury indicted the prisoners, and their trial ended in mid-June after the jury was out twelve minutes. Judge J. D. Foster sentenced Myers and Brown to hang; Theodore Mitchell pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and received thirty years. Sheriff Walters hanged Myers and Brown at New Madrid on July 15 before a crowd reported at five thousand, some arriving by excursion boat from Cairo. No report of action against the would-be lynchers appears in the coverage; the Hickman correspondent noted "much indignation" at the sheriff's action instead.

The Hickman Courier reported it in a farm-news letter, using the stock phrase "Judge Lynch" and recording local anger at the sheriff rather than at the would-be lynchers. A one-sentence wire item ran among national crime notes as far away as Dakota and Wisconsin, while a Missouri dispatch cited the fear of lynching only to explain the governor's order.

No report named the race of the prisoners or of the crowd, though the Sedalia Weekly Bazoo described both men as blue-eyed and Myers as light-haired. Coverage of the July execution celebrated swift legal punishment: the Memphis Daily Appeal headlined it "Not a Whit Too Soon," and the Sedalia paper praised the region's "grim expedition" in punishing the gang.

A June 2 summary in the Princeton Union stated that the captured men "were afterward hung by a mob," which the later trial and execution reports contradict. The Hickman letter said the gang had killed the Wayne County sheriff and deputy, while July accounts said Davis and Hatton recovered. Accounts also differ on whether the sheriff acted on his own or on the governor's order, and whether the steamer landed the prisoners at Cairo or St. Louis.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Jesse Myers and Frank Brown
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A mob or 'lynching parties' organized to hang two jailed prisoners at New Madrid, and the sheriff removed them before it acted, so this is a threatened lynching with no one killed (A1, A5, A7, A13).

The crowd planned to hang the prisoners 'in haste and try them at leisure' for the murders they were accused of, but the sheriff took them away first and no one was killed by the mob (A5, A1); Myers and Brown were later hanged legally after a trial (A8, A9).

A Kentucky correspondent's letter (A5), a wire paragraph (A1), a Poplar Bluff dispatch (A7) and the Sedalia account (A13) independently report the lynching danger and the removal of the prisoners from New Madrid.
